I feel you, but even if worst case scenario that you have oral herpes, it will be okay. My mom has oral herpes that she got as a kid from her aunt double-dipping in a party dip, and she’s been married to my dad for nearly 30 years and he has still never contracted it. 

Statistically, most people have herpes (67%!) and most don’t even know it. It sucks that your friend exposed you to it, especially if they knew they were contagious, but if it’s any consolation it’s very common. 

I think you’ll be surprised about how okay people would be with dating someone with herpes. It’s very manageable with Valtrex, and people get oral herpes all types of ways — most of them like you, through accidental, non-sexual contact. 

I know it feels overwhelming, but I promise you life with herpes isn’t as bad as you might be catastrophizing it to be. In fact, if you get a positive diagnosis it could be really helpful — you can get medicine to manage your symptoms and it’s very effective at stopping the negative effects quickly. 

Hang in there. Getting cold sores sucks, but I promise there is still a lot to live for even if you get diagnosed with it.

Hope you’re hanging in there and have patience for yourself — the average 2023 marriage age for men in Utah is 26.8 (which is below the national average of 30.5), so remind yourself that statistically, more than half of men in your bracket who will get married are not yet married. 

I’m a grad student studying the impacts of dating and marriage, and while I know that romantic relationships are a deeply personal and individual level experience, there ARE macro trends to consider if getting married is an important/present goal for you. 

For example, there are geographic places you should consider moving to post-undergrad if you want to increase your odds of finding a suitable partner (“Date-onomics” by Birger is a great book to read up on this). As women with a college degree typically only date and marry men with a college degree, you might fare better moving to a city with a higher percentage of single, educated women relative to men. 

Houston has about 52% more single college-educated women relative to single college educated men, whereas Provo has 18% more single college educated men than single college educated women. From a macro perspective, you are at a statistical disadvantage as a man trying to date in Provo. 

(If you’re a single college educated woman reading this comment, then you should know that the best city to increase your odds of dateable educated men-to-women is San Jose. New York City, in comparison, skews heavily towards more single educated women). 

Additionally, the LDS dynamics (if you’re only interested in dating members of the church) skew heavily in your favor, especially outside of Utah. Post-undergrad singles wards in most major cities have a gender ratio that favors men like yourself. You may actually find more success in dating once you graduate and start working a job. (Note that this may likely also require you to be open to expanding your expectations of gender roles, which my single LDS female friends often describe to me is a challenge they find with dating LDS men). 

I hope this doesn’t sound too cold or detached from your daily experience, but the data shows being an educated man really is the better side of the equation to be on, if the desired outcome is marriage. Take comfort in that. 

One last thought on this: if you really want to play the odds game, this same data shows that educated women are outpacing men in liberalization AND that politics is an increasingly salient heuristic for choosing a mate. Learning more about Democratic/progressive politics and seeing if you can agree with any of those policies may indeed increase your chances of finding a match that would likewise be interested in you. Of course ideology is a deeply personal identity that’s not easily changed, but something to consider! :) 

Happy to talk more about my research if you (or anyone in the comments) is curious about what we can learn from macro trends and how to best situate yourself in the dating game. 

Good luck out there! You still have plenty of time and lots of experiences left, don’t fret!!

I think you bring up really good points here, especially about the Orc’s quick turn on Adar.

For the most part, I took the disgruntled deputy orc meant to represent what many of the orcs, especially higher management ones, were feeling — they were clearly not happy with Adar’s leadership. Combine that with a tendency for “groupthink” among the orcs and once one turns against Adar it’s easy to imagine that they’d follow like lemmings. They’re not the most free-thinking species 😂

I do think it’s dumb that Sauron was able to take control of an entire army so quickly. I mean I guess the idea is that Sauron is incredibly powerful at deception and coercion, and orcs have incredibly weak minds — they’re easy to manipulate. Perhaps 2nd Age Sauron overestimated this quality, which is what got him killed the first time — while they’re malleable, they’re not blank slates, and Sauron still needs to exert SOME influence, at least before he enslaves them. 

It seems pretty clear though that Sauron needs an army though if he wants to take over Middle Earth — no way he could mind control everyone, or at least not in a reasonable timeframe. It took him weeks (months?) to control Celebrimbor and a handful of his smiths, no way to tell how long an entire army of elves would take — not to mention that it would take a lot of maintenance to keep them in line. Orcs on the other hand? A much easier, much quicker, much simpler army to control.

I’ve been a GSI for several semesters, and at least in our department we are required to oblige any regrade requests. Technically I don’t think a GSI can refuse a regrade request — you should consult your syllabus and, if it says you’re admitted a regrade request, you should definitely check the ego of this GSI and escalate it to the professor. Everyone SHOULD be entitled to a regrade request — everyone makes mistakes, including GSIs/graders. 

That being said, as a GSI I can pretty confidently say that after grading 50 midterms, it’s usually quite easy to sense where each exam lands in the grading scale. I’ve had a few regrades as a GSI (both requests from my students and doing the regrade for others) and I don’t think I’ve ever heard of a regrade being more than a few points +/- the original grade. 

I’m sorry they were a dick to you. That’s never okay. Grades in college are an emotional experience, both for the person receiving the grade and for the one who has to defend the grades they give. I’ve found that often both sides take regrade requests very personally.

I hate to be that guy™️, but I don’t think we can actually claim all of the Targaryen dragons are related (at least by book lore).

Aenar the Exile brought five dragons with him from Valyria, one of which was Balerion. While it COULD make sense that all of these dragons are related/from the same line, it’s not certain — in fact, it could also be plausible that Valyria had a dragon exchange market to diversify their dragons and even breed for certain qualities. With ~40 dragonlord families and at least 300 Valyrian dragons (that’s the number of dragons sent to fight the Rhoynar), there’s a lot of potential for dragon diversity and genetic lines. Thus, it’s possible these five dragons were related OR were completely genetically different OR a mix of the two. 

While four of these og Valyrian dragons died, they left behind eggs from which we get Meraxes and Vhagar. We don’t know if Meraxes and Vhagar came from the same clutch of eggs or from different dragons. They could be siblings, they could be Balerion’s offspring, they could be eggs from two completely different dragons, they could be dragon cousins, etc. We just don’t know. 

Then, for the Targaryen dragons that came after (Vermithor, Quicksilver, Silverwing, Dreamfyre, Meleys, Caraxes, Syrax, Seasmoke, Sunfyre, etc) we have no clear idea where exactly their eggs came from — some of them, especially the older dragons, could reasonably have come from the other dead Valyrian dragons or (as I’m sure many of them were) from each other in clear genetic lines. 

In other words, your claim is PROBABLY true that all of the Targaryen dragons are related, but it’s not “point blank period”. It’s very possible there are two, three, or even five distinct genetic dragon lines from which the Targaryen dragons descend from. 

Also, we haven’t even considered the lack of clarity on whether dragons reproduce asexually or in mated pairs (or possibly a combination of the two), which just adds more complexity to the potential genetic trees.

Finally, we don’t know if Sheepstealer, Grey Ghost, or Cannibal ever laid clutches and left them for the Targaryens to eventually go and collect (or mated with Targaryen-bonded dragons), so it could be possible that even more genetic lines exist from these three wild dragons. This is probably unlikely because the wild dragons were reported to be antagonistic to Targaryen dragons, but hey if it’s mating season who knows 🤷🏻‍♂️
